梅樂頓1963年於英格蘭伯明罕發展，源自加州哈利·錢柏林的鍵盤磁帶樂器。1962: The Mellotron was developed in Birmingham, England, in 1963, from the keyboard tape instrument of Harry Chamberlin in California. In 1962 Chamberlin's sales agent Bill Fransen brought two to England to look for a maker of tape heads; the Bradley brothers thought the design could be improved and brought it out with Eric Robinson and David Nixon. The early domestic models included automatic accompaniment; in the mid and late 1960s it entered rock and pop, and in the 1970s it was common in progressive rock. In 1970 a 35-key model with a detachable tape frame was introduced for touring; production stopped in 1986, and in the 1990s it revived through use by bands, which led the original company to reopen.
梅樂頓主體採用木質外殼與金屬框架構成；鍵盤為塑膠或象牙質鍵；內部核心為多條磁帶纏: The main body of the Mellotron is a wooden case with a metal frame; the keys are plastic or ivory; at its core are many lengths of tape wound on metal pulleys and a playback-head assembly; the motor and spring mechanism are of metal; the tape is an acetate film with an iron-oxide magnetic coating; the interior holds several playback heads, drive gears and electronic amplifier circuit boards, together forming a complex electromechanical system.
梅樂頓以類比錄音磁帶發聲，按下琴鍵使磁帶經轉軸通過播放頭，放開後由彈簧收回。每次: The Mellotron sounds from analogue recording tape: pressing a key brings the tape past the playback head on a capstan, and a spring pulls it back when the key is released. Each playback produces a slight waver of pitch and a fluctuation of volume, so the same note is a little different every time. The harder the key is pressed, the tighter the tape touches the playback head, which allows aftertouch; pressing too many keys at once drags the motor and the pitch falls flat. The early tapes from Chamberlin were based on three violins, with a range of about G3 to F6, and the other sounds are limited by the range of the original recordings. The idea is close to that of a sampler, but the sound comes from physical tape.
梅樂頓早期用於家庭與俱樂部，後進入搖滾與流行音樂，如曼弗雷德·曼恩〈Semi-D: The Mellotron was used early on in homes and clubs, and later entered rock and pop, for example Manfred Mann's 〈Semi-Detached, Suburban Mr. James〉, the Beatles' 〈Strawberry Fields Forever〉 and David Bowie's 〈Space Oddity〉. In the 1970s it was common in progressive rock and was also used by touring players; in the 1990s it was used by bands such as Oasis, the Smashing Pumpkins, Muse and Radiohead.
梅樂頓（Mellotron）是1963年於英國伯明翰發展的電動機械式鍵盤樂器，H: The Mellotron is an electromechanical keyboard instrument developed in Birmingham in England in 1963, Hornbostel–Sachs number 524. When the player presses a key, the tape presses against the capstan and is drawn across the playback head to sound; when the key is released a spring pulls the tape back, and different sections of tape give different timbres. Early models were aimed at the home and the club, and later portable models were used by touring players; it is common in rock, pop and progressive rock line-ups.
